title: Pluralising the فَاعِل, the Feminine Plural يَفْعَلْنَ, and حَرْف الاسْتِقْبَال سَـ versus سَوْفَ
summary: Working through the tamrīnāt of lesson eleven from page 76, the class converts singular sentences to plural, then switches male doers to female and adjusts each verb to match. The heart of the session is the third-person feminine plural مُضَارِع, which unexpectedly takes a يَـ prefix with a نَ ending (يَعْرِفْنَ), and the closing stretch introduces حَرْف الاسْتِقْبَال (ḥarf al-istiqbāl : the particle of futurity), distinguishing the near future سَـ from the more distant سَوْفَ.
key_points: A noun on the pattern فَاعِل (fāʿil) — the اسْم الفَاعِل — usually pluralises to فَاعِلُونَ: صَائِم (ṣāʾim) becomes صَائِمُونَ (ṣāʾimūna : those fasting). The teacher offered this as a reliable guess, not an absolute rule.

The third-person feminine plural مُضَارِع takes a يَـ prefix and a نَ ending — يَعْرِفْنَ (yaʿrifna : they f. know), يَكْتُبْنَ (yaktubna : they f. write) — even though the feminine singular takes تَـ (تَعْرِفُ). This shift from تَـ to يَـ is what makes the form tricky.

تَذْهَبُ (tadhhabu) is identical for the third-person feminine singular (هِيَ تَذْهَبُ : she goes) and the second-person masculine singular (أَنْتَ تَذْهَبُ : you go). Only context tells you which is meant.

Changing a doer from male to female means changing the verb with it, and any attached pronoun too: يَلْعَبُ الطِّفْلُ مَعَ أُخْتِهِ becomes تَلْعَبُ الطِّفْلَةُ مَعَ أُخْتِهَا — three changes in one sentence.
مَا (mā) negates the مَاضِي and لَا (lā) negates the مُضَارِع — مَا كَتَبَ أَحْمَدُ الدَّرْسَ against لَا يَكْتُبُ أَحْمَدُ الدَّرْسَ. The negating particle sits directly before the verb it negates.

حَرْف الاسْتِقْبَال is the letter that points to the future. سَـ indicates the near future (سَأَذْهَبُ : I will go shortly) while سَوْفَ indicates the further future (سَوْفَ أَذْهَبُ : I will go after some time).
To say something has already happened, add قَدْ (qad) to the مَاضِي rather than using a future particle.
When the verb comes before its plural doer it stays singular; when it follows the doer it is made plural — and this holds for the مُضَارِع just as for the مَاضِي.

Vocabulary covered in the drills: مِكْنَسَة (miknasah : broom), بَحَثَ عَنْ (baḥatha ʿan : to search for), غَسَلَ (ghasala : to wash), حَلَّاق (ḥallāq : barber), مَحَطَّة (maḥaṭṭah : station or stop), الْقَادِمَة (al-qādimah : the next), غَدًا (ghadan : tomorrow), and كُرَة الْقَدَم (kurat al-qadam : football), literally the ball of the foot.
أَسْئِلَة (asʾilah : questions) is the plural of سُؤَال (suʾāl), from سَأَلَ (saʾala : to ask), and كَثِيرَة (kathīrah) means many.
questions: [00:03:00] Q: Why is the plural sometimes مُسْلِمُونَ and sometimes something else? — A: There is a reason for the variation and it will be covered later; for now, a word on the فَاعِل pattern can be guessed as فَاعِلُونَ.
[00:06:02] Q: Shouldn't the feminine plural be يَبْحَثُونَ? — A: No, that is the masculine plural; the feminine plural is يَبْحَثْنَ, as the chart shows.
[00:11:00] Q: Why is there no تَـ on يَعْرِفْنَ? — A: The تَـ is dropped in the plural: the feminine singular is تَعْرِفُ, but the feminine plural changes to يَـ, giving يَعْرِفْنَ.
[00:14:00] Q: What does مَعَ do to the word after it? — A: It is a ظَرْف (ẓarf) rather than a حَرْف الجَرّ, and the word following it is put in the genitive.

[00:25:00] Q: What is the difference between saying he wrote and he was writing? — A: Was writing carries a sense of continuation; the plain مَاضِي here just means he wrote. The construction for the continuous past comes later.

[00:35:00] Q: What is the difference between سَأَذْهَبُ and سَوْفَ أَذْهَبُ? — A: سَـ is the near future and سَوْفَ is the farther future, meaning after some time — as in كَلَّا سَيَعْلَمُونَ, they will know soon.
[00:45:01] Q: How do I say I have already gone? — A: Add قَدْ and keep the verb in the past tense, rather than using a future particle.
[00:47:00] Q: How do I say I am getting off at the next stop? — A: سَأَنْزِلُ فِي الْمَحَطَّةِ الْقَادِمَةِ.

quiz.q: What is the third-person feminine plural مُضَارِع of عَرَفَ?
quiz.a: The feminine plural takes a يَـ prefix with a نَ ending: يَعْرِفْنَ. The teacher stressed this because the feminine singular uses تَـ instead.

quiz.q: Why did the teacher call the feminine plural form tricky?
options: Because it drops the final نَ
Because the feminine singular uses تَـ but the feminine plural switches to يَـ
Because it is identical to the masculine plural
quiz.a: تَعْرِفُ for the feminine singular but يَعْرِفْنَ for the feminine plural — the prefix changes where students expect it to stay.

quiz.q: The form تَذْهَبُ can refer to which two persons?
options: Third-person feminine singular and second-person masculine singular
First-person singular and third-person masculine singular
Third-person masculine plural and feminine plural
Second-person feminine plural and third-person feminine plural
quiz.a: هِيَ تَذْهَبُ and أَنْتَ تَذْهَبُ share the same form, so only context distinguishes them — the whole point of tamrīn 8.

quiz.q: Turning يَلْعَبُ الطِّفْلُ مَعَ أُخْتِهِ feminine, how many words must change?
options: Two, the noun and the verb
Three, the noun, the verb, and the attached pronoun
quiz.a: The teacher counted three: طِفْل becomes طِفْلَة, يَلْعَبُ becomes تَلْعَبُ, and أُخْتِهِ becomes أُخْتِهَا.

quiz.q: Which is the correct negation of أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ?
quiz.a: أَشْرَبُ is مُضَارِع, so it is negated with لَا; مَا is reserved for the مَاضِي.
The teacher derived it from مُسْتَقْبَل (future), so it is the letter pointing toward the future — the سِين.

quiz.q: Which conveys the more distant future?
quiz.a: سَـ is the near future and سَوْفَ means after some time, which is how the teacher separated the two.

quiz.q: How do you express that an action has already taken place?
quiz.a: When a student wanted to say he had already gone, the teacher told him to add قَدْ and keep the past tense.
Introduced as a new word in tamrīn 6: مِكْنَسَة is a broom, and the sentence had the sisters searching for it.

quiz.q: What does كُرَة الْقَدَم literally mean?
quiz.a: قَدَم is foot, so كُرَة الْقَدَم is literally the ball of the foot — the teacher's aside while translating football.

quran_examples.translation: No! They are going to know. Then no! They are going to know.
quran_examples.note: The teacher's own example for the near future سَـ: سَيَعْلَمُونَ means they will know soon, as against the more distant سَوْفَ.

quran_examples.translation: No! You are going to know.
quran_examples.note: Illustrates سَوْفَ, the particle the teacher contrasted with سَـ as pointing to the further future.

quran_examples.translation: Divorced women shall wait concerning themselves for three monthly periods.
quran_examples.note: Demonstrates the third-person feminine plural مُضَارِع that the class drilled: يَتَرَبَّصْنَ carries the يَـ prefix with the نَ ending, exactly like يَعْرِفْنَ.

quran_examples.arabic: أَمَّا السَّفِينَةُ فَكَانَتْ لِمَسَاكِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ فِي الْبَحْرِ
quran_examples.transliteration: ammā al-safīnatu fa-kānat li-masākīna yaʿmalūna fī al-baḥr
quran_examples.translation: As for the ship, it belonged to poor people working at sea.
